Front: From what does an agent select which tool to use?
Back: From the tools' names, descriptions, parameter schemas, and examples - tool design is prompt design plus API design.

Front: List the things a good tool description should explain.
Back: What the tool does, when to use it, when not to use it, required input formats, what the output contains, and important limitations and safety concerns.

Front: When are input_examples especially helpful in a tool definition?
Back: For nested objects, date formats, identifiers, and domain-specific enums, where a schema alone is ambiguous.

Front: Why use an enum instead of a free-text string for a closed set like a repository source?
Back: Enums encode stable closed sets so the model picks a valid option; free text increases ambiguity and invalid values.

Front: Describe the lookup-then-act pattern for ambiguous entity names.
Back: First a search tool returns IDs and distinguishing metadata; then the action tool operates only on an unambiguous ID, so the model never acts on a guessed name.

Front: A project lookup returns several candidates the agent cannot confidently choose between before a destructive op. Best design?
Back: Present the candidates to the user with differentiating fields and let them select one; a single-click confirmation beats asking the model to guess and run a destructive operation.

Front: How does disambiguation differ from preview-then-execute?
Back: Disambiguation resolves which entity the user means; preview-then-execute confirms what action will happen to it - they are complementary, not substitutes.

Front: If the user already has a device_id, why should a downstream tool accept device_id directly?
Back: Prefer stable identifiers over derived intermediate values; making the tool resolve mechanical dependencies internally avoids an unnecessary lookup and its failure coupling.

Front: Why split a single log_workout(type,value,unit) tool into log_cardio_session and log_strength_session?
Back: When parameters have interdependent constraints, separate tools make the schema itself encode the distinction and prevent invalid combinations.

Front: Why replace a unified manage_order(action,...) tool with separate operation tools?
Back: When operations have different required fields, a unified tool causes omitted parameters and irrelevant fields; separate tools give a simpler choice and cleaner schema.

Front: What makes a tool output good for the next decision?
Back: It is structured, compact, and includes identifiers downstream tools can use - not human-readable prose alone.

Front: Three carriers represent shipment status differently. What should the tool return?
Back: A normalized consistent schema (e.g., status, estimated_delivery, delay_reason, requires_action) rather than forcing the model to learn carrier-specific code mappings.

Front: Should "no matches found" be returned as an isError result?
Back: No. It is a successful result with an empty results array; marking it an error makes the agent retry a valid query as though the tool failed.

Front: How should a tool handle a paginated backend API by default?
Back: Return the first page, a total_count (or estimate), and a cursor/continuation token; do not auto-fetch hundreds of items the user may not need.

Front: Name three good candidates for combining operations into a composite tool.
Back: Mechanical sequences needing no intermediate decision, latency-heavy lookups that always co-occur, and atomic operations where separate calls create race conditions.

Front: When should steps stay separate rather than be combined into a composite tool?
Back: When the model must inspect intermediate results before deciding; selection, judgment, and editorial choice belong outside composite tools.

Front: Why combine check-availability and reserve-slot into one atomic find_and_book tool?
Back: Separate calls risk another user taking the slot between them; an atomic operation prevents that race. A hold_slot tool adds a new race window and an extra step.

Front: Why should a research workflow NOT combine retrieve-sources and write-conclusion?
Back: The model needs to inspect the sources and preserve provenance; hiding that decision point inside a composite tool removes required judgment.

Front: Why does auto-fetching every page of an external API usually hurt?
Back: It causes long latency for broad queries, wastes tokens when only the first items are needed, and can blow context on very large result sets.

Front: What happens to tool selection as the number of similar tools grows past a handful?
Back: Accuracy drops noticeably; do not expose dozens of similar tools at once by default.

Front: Describe progressive availability for a large tool set.
Back: Start with discovery tools (e.g., search_available_connectors), return a ranked shortlist, then dynamically add the selected matching tools so the agent uses them on later turns.

Front: Why is a monolithic find_and_execute tool worse than a discovery tool plus separate execution?
Back: Search-and-execute hides the final decision and can perform the wrong action too early; discovery should narrow choices while the agent or user can still inspect before execution.

Front: How does the Claude Agent SDK support progressive tool availability natively?
Back: Through tool search and dynamic tool registration; MCP servers can also send list_changed notifications so clients refresh tools without reconnecting.

Front: When tool outputs include ML confidence scores, what should the tool return besides raw confidence?
Back: A derived requires_review boolean with review_reasons, calibrated against a labeled validation set, so agent behavior is consistent instead of over-trusting or over-escalating raw scores.

Front: Why is "Ready to post. Confirm?" with no details an unsafe confirmation prompt?
Back: The tool must return enough structured detail (cost, target, schedule, irreversible effects, scope) for the user to catch a mistake, even if users usually click yes.

Front: Why is dry_run: boolean on a single tool insufficient for a must-always-preview destructive action?
Back: The model can simply call the tool with dry_run=false; use a structural preview-token-execute pattern instead.

Front: Describe the three-step structural pattern for a mandatory-preview workspace deletion.
Back: preview_delete_workspace returns impact plus a one-time confirmation token; the user reviews; execute_delete_workspace requires the token and verifies it matches the previewed action.

Front: Do MCP tool annotations or descriptions enforce security?
Back: No. Security belongs in code, hooks, permissions, and tool logic; annotations and descriptions are untrusted hints.

Front: Why is encoding format hints in parameter names (e.g., date_string_iso_yyyy_mm_dd) a pitfall?
Back: Format belongs in descriptions and schemas, not names; making everything a free-text string increases ambiguity and invalid combinations.

Front: List the tool-error categories and the correct handling for each.
Back: Transient infrastructure: retry in tool with backoff; permanent validation: return structured details to correct or ask; business rule: non-retryable with user explanation; permission: non-retryable with escalation path; uncertain write state: report uncertainty, no auto-retry.

Front: If a read-only API times out and immediate retries usually succeed, where should retry happen?
Back: Inside the tool - it should absorb recoverable infrastructure noise; the model does not need to see the first failed network attempt.

Front: Why must a payment/notification/order timeout after submission NOT be auto-retried?
Back: The tool may not know whether the side effect occurred; blind retry causes duplicate charges, messages, or postings. Report uncertain state and require an idempotency key or user decision.

Front: How should application-level tool errors be returned in MCP?
Back: As normal tool results with isError: true, not uncaught exceptions; protocol-level failures use JSON-RPC errors.

Front: Distinguish MCP protocol errors from tool execution errors.
Back: Protocol errors mean the request could not be processed at the protocol boundary (unknown tool, malformed JSON-RPC, missing required parameter). Tool execution errors mean the tool ran but the operation failed (404, 503, business rule, permission, rate limit) and use isError: true.

Front: A check_availability(user_email) call omits user_email entirely. Protocol error or isError?
Back: A JSON-RPC protocol error - the call was not even structurally well-formed against the schema.

Front: The calendar API returns 404 because the user does not exist. Protocol error or isError?
Back: A tool execution error with isError: true - the tool was invoked correctly; the operation simply failed. A missing record is data, not a protocol failure.

Front: Why is putting a missing-required-parameter failure in isError a bug?
Back: It confuses the agent into retrying with the same bad call; a structural protocol violation should be a JSON-RPC error so the agent does not blindly retry.

Front: Why is putting a remote 503 into a JSON-RPC protocol error a bug?
Back: It prevents the agent from trying again later; a transient upstream failure should be isError: true so the agent can decide to retry, switch tools, or escalate.

Front: Where should retry logic live when the model needs to change inputs or strategy?
Back: At the model level - validation errors, syntax errors in user filters, or a wrong identifier require the model to change the request, not a silent tool retry.

Front: A search_catalog tool has 8% transient timeouts and 4% user-filter syntax errors. Correct design?
Back: Retry the transient errors inside the tool with backoff and surface only the final outcome; surface syntax errors immediately with parameter validation details so the model can correct or ask the user.

Front: Why is a retryable: true|false boolean alone weaker than actually retrying transient failures in the tool?
Back: It still costs a model turn and risks the agent retrying anyway; actually retrying transient failures inside the tool is more reliable.

Front: For a write timeout of uncertain state, should the result be flagged retry_safe: true?
Back: No. Mark it an error, communicate that delivery is unknown and may have occurred, and encourage a separate status lookup or user confirmation before acting.

Front: What are MCP's three server-side building blocks and who controls each?
Back: Tools (model-controlled actions), resources (application-controlled context), and prompts (user/application-controlled reusable templates).

Front: Should a database schema or API spec the agent consults before acting be a resource or a tool?
Back: A resource - it is stable reference material the agent reads like context; dynamic state requiring live computation should be a tool.

Front: Why are MCP resources and tools complements rather than alternatives?
Back: Resources describe what is true and stable; tools describe what actions can be taken. Replacing resources with tools forces a call to learn anything; replacing tools with resources prevents acting at all.

Front: When is exposing data through an MCP server more valuable than a custom in-app tool?
Back: When the integration should be reusable across multiple clients or applications; a deeply app-specific one-off workflow may be simpler as a custom tool.

Front: Does MCP automatically solve authentication, rate limiting, retries, or caching?
Back: No - those remain system design responsibilities; MCP is a protocol, not a complete middleware platform.

Front: An agent ignores a specialized MCP tool and uses generic search instead. Most likely fix?
Back: Improve the MCP tool description: explain when it is preferable to generic alternatives, describe inputs/outputs, add examples, and mention key capabilities - do not remove all competing tools.

Front: Name the four standard MCP tool annotation hints.
Back: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint - hints that help the host build UI affordances but are not a security boundary.

Front: How should a host treat a server advertising readOnlyHint: true on a destructive tool?
Back: As an untrusted hint: use annotations to choose which prompt to show but never to skip a security check policy requires; base permission decisions on server trust, user policy, tool identity, and real risk.
